stories.headline: Update: U.S. Blockades Strait of Hormuz as Iran Seizes Cargo Ships, Ceasefire Expires
stories.summary:
The U.S.-Iran conflict entered a critical new phase after a 60-day ceasefire expired Monday with no diplomatic or military off-ramp in sight. Iran seized two cargo ships in the Strait of Hormuz, including the Epaminondas, while President Trump announced the U.S. is blockading the strait — one of the world's most vital shipping chokepoints through which roughly a fifth of global oil supply passes.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a new round of sanctions Monday aimed at cutting Iran off from all sources of revenue, warning every nation that does business with Tehran to sever those ties or face U.S. retaliation. Despite Trump's earlier promise of an 'economic D-Day,' the announcement was short on specifics and stopped short of immediately imposing secondary sanctions on trading partners such as China, Turkey, and the UAE. Bessent said he wanted those countries to have time to disengage, adding: 'Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?'

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday he was not ruling out resuming military strikes against Iran, even as officials acknowledged diminishing stockpiles of key weapons have pushed the administration toward economic warfare. Energy markets have experienced wild swings since the initial U.S.-Israel attack on Iran on February 28, and the strait seizures threaten further disruption to global oil and supply chains.

Iran's top negotiator signaled Tehran intends to control passage through the Strait of Hormuz, and the Iranian rial fell to a record low of 2.02 million to the dollar as currency markets opened Monday. The conflict has drawn in regional actors, with Iran's parliament speaker meeting Pakistan's army chief in Tehran, and analysts warn the combination of naval confrontation, economic pressure, and expiring diplomacy makes the coming days among the most consequential of the six-month-old conflict.

stories.headline: Russia Threatens 'Semi-Military' Attacks on UK Drone Factories After Missile Blueprint Transfer
stories.summary:
A former Russian deputy foreign minister has warned that UK factories producing drones for Ukraine could face attacks from 'unknown sources' following Britain's decision to share blueprints for components of the Scalp cruise missile — a French variant of the UK's Storm Shadow — allowing Ukraine to manufacture the long-range weapon domestically. Andrei Fedorov, a pro-Kremlin commentator, told BBC Newsnight that President Putin faces 'serious pressure' to respond and that a 'semi-military' response could take the form of factory attacks not directly attributed to Russia.

The warning came as newly installed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham returned from his first foreign trip to Kyiv, where he met President Zelensky, chaired a meeting of the 'coalition of the willing,' and reaffirmed Britain's commitment to Ukraine's defense. Burnham announced plans to travel to Washington next month alongside European leaders to lobby President Trump over Ukraine's defense needs, his first visit to the U.S. since taking office.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov separately said Moscow's military was already gathering data to locate missile production sites for potential destruction, and accused Britain of adding 'fuel to the fire.' Burnham dismissed the criticism, responding: 'Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?'

The blueprint transfer carries strategic significance beyond the UK-Russia dynamic: Ukraine faces critically low stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles due to U.S. supplies being diverted to the Iran conflict, leaving it increasingly vulnerable ahead of a winter during which Russia is expected to intensify strikes on energy infrastructure. Zelensky has said he hopes to secure 300 Patriot missiles before winter.

stories.headline: Lockerbie Bombing Trial Postponed a Third Time After New Evidence Surfaces
stories.summary:
The trial of Libyan suspect Abu Agila Mohammad Kheir Al-Marimi over the 1988 Lockerbie bombing has been postponed for a third time, just days before jury selection was set to begin in Washington, D.C. on Wednesday. The delay came after 'newly discovered evidence' previously unknown to both the defense and federal prosecutors emerged on Friday, August 21, prompting Al-Marimi's legal team to seek more time. A new trial date has been set for January 2027.

Trial judge Dabney Friedrich granted the postponement, a decision that underscores the significance of the new material given the months of preparation and extensive pre-trial legal battles that had already taken place. Al-Marimi, who has been in U.S. custody since 2022, has denied building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing all 259 people aboard and 11 on the ground — 190 of them American.

The case is the culmination of a nearly four-decade joint investigation by Scottish and U.S. authorities. Scottish prosecutors and Police Scotland detectives had been scheduled to travel to Washington to participate in the proceedings, with Scottish witnesses among those expected to testify first.

The Crown Office's head of the Lockerbie investigation acknowledged the adjournment 'will be disappointing for the families' of victims, who have waited nearly 38 years for a verdict. The bombing remains the deadliest terrorist attack and mass murder in British history, and for many victim families, justice has remained frustratingly out of reach through multiple delays and decades of legal proceedings.

stories.headline: Tornado Tears Through French Village, Injuring 39 and Destroying Hundreds of Homes
stories.summary:
A tornado struck the village of Pomas in southwestern France on Monday, injuring 39 people, damaging an estimated 300 homes, and leaving roughly 2,800 households across 10 villages without electricity. Winds reaching 117 km/h (73 mph) tore roofs from houses, toppled trees, and partially collapsed a medieval castle whose stones had stood for a thousand years. Fifteen people were taken to hospital, with two in critical condition.

More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the area south of Carcassonne in the Aude region. Residents described the tornado as a 'huge red and yellow chimney' and said the destruction was near-total in parts of the village. One man said his pregnant wife was injured when their house collapsed around her.

The extreme weather also forced the cancellation of the third stage of the Vuelta a España cycling race, which was taking place in the same region when a hailstorm forced riders to take shelter roughly 15 kilometers from the finish line. Flight delays and cancellations were reported at multiple major French airports including Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, and Toulouse.

French authorities had issued orange storm alerts for large parts of the southwest before the tornado struck. The event is the latest in a summer of severe weather across Europe, which has seen unprecedented heatwaves, large wildfires, and now destructive storms — France's southwest alone saw one of its largest wildfires since World War Two earlier this season.
